issues.legal_issue: A tenant parts with legal possession when another person has exclusive possession and the tenant retains neither control of the premises nor the right to possess them.
material_facts: The tenant's son carried on a sole-proprietary business in the rented shop and had exclusive possession of it.
The tenant had no interest in that business, worked at another shop, and had not retained control of the rented shop.
The tenant was occasionally seen sitting in the shop, but there was no plea of concurrent use or of the son occupying as a licensee while the tenant retained possession.
The tenant did not plead that he had obtained the landlord's written consent.
issues.conclusion: The tenant had parted with legal possession of the shop, bringing the case within the ground for eviction under Section 14(1)(b) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958; the appeal was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 14(1)(b), as explained in Jagan Nath (deceased) through L.Rs. v. Chander Bhan & Ors., parting with possession requires the tenant to vest possession in another and divest himself of both physical possession and the right to possession. Another person's use of the premises alone is insufficient if the tenant retains legal possession.

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding: The proceeding seeks recovery of rented premises on the ground that the tenant transferred possession to another person.
predicates.another_person_has_exclusive_possession: A person other than the tenant has exclusive possession of the premises.
predicates.tenant_retains_no_right_or_control: The tenant has retained neither the right to possess the premises nor control over them.

issues.definition: When an eviction proceeding concerns a transfer of rented premises, another person's exclusive possession amounts to the tenant parting with legal possession if the tenant retains neither the right to possess nor control.

issues.legal_issue: Implied permission or acquiescence does not satisfy a requirement that the landlord's consent to parting with possession be in writing.
material_facts: The alleged parting with possession was the subject of a rent-control eviction petition.

There was evidence that the landlord had seen the son's business sign from 1972 and had seen the son sitting in the shop from 1968, but no positive evidence established when the landlord learned that the son had exclusive possession and was carrying on business as sole proprietor.
The tenant did not establish written consent to the parting with possession.
issues.conclusion: Mere permission, acquiescence, or implied consent cannot replace the written consent required by Section 14(1)(b); the consent must relate to the specific parting with possession.
issues.legal_principle: Section 14(1)(b) requires the landlord's consent in writing. M/s Shalimar Tar Products Ltd. v. H.C. Sharma & Ors. explains that this requirement serves the public purpose of avoiding disputes about consent, so implied consent or acquiescence is insufficient. The Court also relied on the distinction between written consent and mere consent, under which implied consent does not arise when the statute requires consent in writing.

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding: The proceeding seeks recovery of rented premises on the ground that the tenant transferred possession to another person.
predicates.tenant_parts_with_possession: The tenant has transferred possession of all or part of the rented premises to another person.
predicates.written_landlord_consent_absent: The tenant has no written consent from the landlord for that transfer.

issues.definition: In a rent-control eviction proceeding, when the tenant transfers possession without written landlord consent, implied consent or acquiescence does not satisfy the written-consent requirement.

issues.legal_issue: A claim that the landlord waived the right to seek eviction for parting with possession is not established without proof that the landlord knew the facts enabling enforcement of that right.
material_facts: The landlord had seen the son sitting in the shop and had seen the business sign, but there was no positive evidence showing when the landlord learned that the son had exclusive possession and operated the business as sole proprietor.
The lower courts had made no definite finding about when the landlord learned of the parting with possession or whether rent was accepted after that knowledge.
The waiver argument was not raised in that form in the courts below and was raised for the first time in the Supreme Court.
issues.conclusion: The Court did not permit the waiver point to be raised for the first time in the appeal and held that the evidence did not establish the landlord's knowledge necessary to support waiver.
issues.legal_principle: Associated Hotels of India Ltd., Delhi v. S.B. Sardar Ranjit Singh states that waiver is the intentional relinquishment of a known right and requires full knowledge of the right and of facts enabling effective action to enforce it. The Court also held that the factual waiver issue could not be considered when raised for the first time in the Supreme Court without findings below. Independently, Section 14(1)(b) requires written consent, and implied consent cannot substitute for it.

predicates.rent_control_eviction_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal in a rent-control eviction case.
predicates.tenant_claims_landlord_waived_eviction_r: The tenant relies on the landlord's conduct as a waiver of the right to seek eviction for transferred possession.
predicates.landlord_knowledge_of_exclusive_transfer: The evidence does not establish when the landlord learned that another person had exclusive possession of the premises.

issues.definition: In a rent-control eviction appeal, a tenant's waiver claim is not established when the landlord's knowledge of the exclusive transfer is unproven.

issues.legal_issue: Evidence of a person's statements in official records may be considered without producing the records when it is not offered to prove the terms of a document or another matter required by law to be documented.
material_facts: Departmental officials testified that official records identified the tenant's son as the son of the person who allegedly adopted him.
The testimony concerned information the son had given in connection with property ownership and applications for licences.
The evidence was not offered to prove the terms of a contract, grant, disposition of property, or a matter required by law to be reduced to writing.
issues.conclusion: The officials' testimony was admissible without production of the underlying record extracts, although it might have had little evidentiary value without those extracts.
issues.legal_principle: Section 91 of the Evidence Act requires the document itself, or admissible secondary evidence, to prove the terms of a contract, grant, or other disposition of property reduced to writing, or a matter required by law to be documented. Relying on Bai Hira Devi & Ors. v. The Official Assignee of Bombay, the Court held that the rule did not exclude the testimony here because it was not offered to prove such documentary terms.

predicates.court_proceeding_involves_testimony_abou: A court proceeding includes testimony concerning information recorded by a public department.
predicates.testimony_reports_a_persons_recorded_sta: A witness reports statements a person made to a public department in connection with that person's dealings or applications.
predicates.document_terms_are_not_being_proved: The testimony is not offered to prove the terms of a written contract, grant, disposition, or a matter required by law to be documented.

issues.definition: Testimony reporting a person's statements recorded by a public department is admissible without the record extracts when the testimony is not offered to prove matters that must be proved through a document.

issues.legal_issue: Evidence concerning an alleged adoption may be considered for the limited purpose of assessing whether a tenant retained control or possession without establishing the adoption's formal validity.
material_facts: The tenant disputed that his son had been adopted by another person and argued that the required formal ceremony of giving and taking had not been proved.

The son carried on business in the rented premises as sole proprietor, and the tenant had not pleaded that they constituted a joint family, were in joint possession, or carried on a joint-family business.
Evidence from official records referred to the son as the child of the alleged adoptive parent.
issues.conclusion: The Court did not need to treat the evidence as proof of a valid adoption under Hindu law; it could be considered to show that no presumption of a joint Hindu family between the tenant and his natural son could be invoked and to assess whether the tenant retained control of the premises.
issues.legal_principle: Lakshman Singh Kothari v. Smt. Rup Kanwar describes the formal giving-and-taking requirement for a valid adoption under Hindu law. The Court did not decide adoption validity on that basis; it treated the evidence as relevant to possession and control and noted the absence of a specific joint-family or joint-possession plea.

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding: The proceeding concerns whether a tenant transferred possession of rented premises.
predicates.adoption_is_relied_on_as_context_for_pos: Evidence concerning an alleged adoption is presented as relevant to the relationship between the tenant and the person occupying the premises.
predicates.joint_family_or_joint_possession_is_not_: The tenant has not specifically pleaded that the occupants constitute a joint family or are in joint possession.

issues.definition: In a rent-control possession dispute, evidence concerning an alleged adoption may be considered as context for possession when joint-family or joint-possession status is not pleaded, without proving that the adoption was valid.
